demand.reason: Global tellurium consumption is about 1,000 metric tons of refined output in 2025, placing it securely within the modest-demand band of 500–10,000 tons.

growth.reason: Demand is projected for high growth (12%+ CAGR) because solar cells now represent 70% of global tellurium consumption, driven by First Solar expanding US utility capacity to 14 GW/year. This rapid expansion in a major energy sector satisfies the maximum framework projection.

supplier_concentration.reason:
Mining: Tellurium has no primary mines and is recovered purely as a byproduct of copper anode slimes. Copper mine production is globally distributed, with no single nation exceeding 30% of global output (Score 1).


Refining: Downstream chemical separation is heavily concentrated. China refined 800 of about 1,000 tons in 2025 (80%), placing refining concentration in the 65–85% band (Score 4).

reserves.reason:
Time-frame: Global economic reserves are estimated at 38,000 tons. At about 1,000 tons a year of refined output, these reserves represent about 38 years of supply, within the 30–50 year band. (USGS no longer quantifies tellurium reserves; 38,000 tons is an older estimate.)


Diversification: Tellurium is recovered from copper anode slime, so its reserves follow copper reserves, which are widely spread (Chile holds 18% of the world total; HHI about 0.08–0.12), below 0.15 (Score 1). China's 80% share of refined tellurium is scored under supplier concentration.

end_use.reason:
Energy Generation & Grid (+1.5): CdTe thin-film solar power cells represent 70% of global tellurium consumption. Defense & National Security (+1.5): HgCdTe infrared detectors are strategically critical for military night-vision and thermal target tracking. Advanced Semiconductors & Computing (+1.0): utilized widely in bismuth telluride thermoelectric devices and semiconductor doping. Construction & Heavy Industry (+0.5): used as a free-machining alloy additive in steels and rubber vulcanization.


Sector presence scores total 4.5 across 4 qualifying sectors. The breadth bonus adds +1.5, yielding an objective composite score of 6.0.

substitutability_recyclability.reason:
Substitutability: Amorphous silicon and CIGS solar cells are commercially deployed substitutes, but they introduce notable cost and efficiency trade-offs. For military long-wave infrared detectors, HgCdTe has no drop-in performance substitute, matching Score 3.


Recyclability: Tellurium recycling from CdTe solar cells remains limited because current panels have not reached the end of their useful lifespans. End-of-life recovery is less than 5% globally, placing it securely in the negligible recycling tier (<5%).

extraction_refining.reason: Tellurium extraction requires processing complex copper electrolytic anode slimes via multi-stage hydrometallurgical roasting, acid leaching, and specialized solvent extraction cascades. High-purity semiconductor refining requires vacuum distillation, restricting operations to fewer than 10-15 facilities globally.

upcoming_projects.reason: The supply pipeline is minimal and structurally constrained. Tellurium cannot be mined independently and relies entirely on copper smelting expansions, which are advancing at modest rates with <5% near-term capacity additions expected.

india_position.reason:
Import Dependence: India has no confirmed commercial tellurium output (Hindalco lists CSIR-IMMT's slime-recovery process as implemented, but publishes no volumes), rendering its expanding solar and advanced component industries 100% import-dependent (Score 5).


Strategic Posture: Tellurium is recognized on India's critical minerals list with customs duties exempted. However, lacking foreign asset equity holdings or specific KABIL mandates, India's posture aligns with declared strategic intent at an early stage (Score 3).

price_volatility.reason: Tellurium prices experienced extreme market breakdown, surging 84% in Europe and 60% in the US within a single year following China's February 2025 export licensing restrictions. Active trade restrictions by a dominant single actor trigger the maximum volatility score.

capability.name: Tellurium
capability.next_move: Publish and scale Hindalco's copper telluride recovery at Dahej, add a circuit at Kutch Copper, and refine to 5N for cadmium telluride.
capability.what_india_has: Hindalco's process at Dahej recovers tellurium from slime leachate as copper telluride (no volumes published); Kutch Copper's slime; high-purity tellurium at the Nuclear Fuel Complex; First Solar's 3.3 GW plant as a buyer.
capability.cost: A circuit is cheap: US$2.9 m for about 20 t/yr at Rio Tinto's Kennecott (#7).

stages.world: A by-product of copper; no primary mines.
China 800 of 1,000 t (2025); Russia 67 t; Japan 61 t; Sweden 48 t.
stages.india: Copper telluride at Hindalco Dahej. USGS says India may refine some tellurium but has no figures; Hindustan Copper last reported it in 2004-05.
The Nuclear Fuel Complex makes high-purity tellurium in small lots; none is made into cadmium telluride.

stages.world: Cadmium telluride solar, thermoelectrics, free-machining alloys.
stages.india: First Solar's 3.3 GW plant in Tamil Nadu, which also recovers tellurium from scrap modules; 2 t imported in 2022-23.

strategyList.name: Copper smelting and anode-slime treatment
strategyList.what: Smelting concentrate, electrorefining copper, then treating anode slime for gold, silver, selenium, tellurium and PGMs.
strategyList.outside_china: China 48% of refined copper; DRC, Chile, Japan. Tellurium from slime: Japan, Russia, Sweden, Canada, US (Rio Tinto).
strategyList.cost: Kutch Copper phase 1: ~US$1.2 bn for 0.5 Mt/yr. Tellurium circuit at Kennecott: US$2.9 m for ~20 t/yr.
strategyList.india_base: Hindalco (Dahej), Kutch Copper (0.5 Mt/yr), Vedanta (Silvassa); CSIR-IMMT's tellurium process listed at Hindalco.
strategyList.gap: Concentrate supply; commercial tellurium circuits and 5N refining.

chemistryList.name: High-purity and electronic materials
chemistryList.who: C-MET (6N gallium); NFC (special materials); CSIR-CGCRI (doped fibres).
chemistryList.carries_over_to: 6N-7N gallium and tellurium; Er- and Yb-doped fibres.
chemistryList.summary: Electronic and optical materials turn small quantities of very clean substances into high-value components. India has documented gallium and tellurium purification work and rare-earth-doped optical-fibre technologies. These are distinct chains: metal purity, semiconductor manufacture and fibre-device manufacture should each be assessed on their own evidence.

links.how: Tellurium recovered from copper anode slime, as in the work at Birla Copper, is the feed; C-MET offers 7N tellurium technology, and the purified metal goes into compounds such as CdTe and CdZnTe.

chemistryList.name: Hydrometallurgy and process R&D
chemistryList.carries_over_to: Tellurium from slime; nickel from overburden; magnet and battery recycling; REE separation flowsheets.
chemistryList.summary: Hydrometallurgy dissolves and separates elements into useful products. India has process-development experience, pilot facilities and some industrial transfers. That foundation can support several mineral chains; each feed still needs its own validated flowsheet and commercial case.

links.how: CSIR-IMMT recorded tellurium recovery from Birla Copper's anode slime, and CSIR-NML lists further selenium and tellurium process development.
